name: Core grammar
blurb: Follows the order of Lingua Latina per se illustrata, with original sentences. Starts at the very beginning.

units.title: Where things are
units.blurb: est, sunt, and in + ablative (≈ LLPSI ch. I)
units.intro: To say where something is, Latin uses _in_ plus the ablative case: _in Italiā_ = in Italy. _est_ means 'is' (one thing); _sunt_ means 'are' (several things). Latin has no word for 'a' or 'the'. Word order is flexible, but subject – place – verb is the usual pattern.

units.title: What and where?
units.blurb: Questions with ubi / quid, and 'X is a Y' sentences
units.intro: _ubi_ asks 'where?' and _quid_ asks 'what?'. To say what something is, put two nominatives together with _est_ or _sunt_: _Rōma urbs est_ (Rome is a city). When the subject is plural, the noun that describes it is plural too.

units.title: Big and small
units.blurb: Adjectives that agree with their noun
units.intro: Adjectives like _magnus, -a, -um_ change their endings to match the noun they describe in gender, number and case. _urbs_ is feminine, so _urbs magna_; _fluvius_ is masculine, so _fluvius magnus_; plural: _urbēs magnae_, _fluviī magnī_. The gender comes from the noun, not from how it looks.

units.title: Family and friends
units.blurb: my / your / our, people, and 3rd-declension nouns
units.intro: Possessives like _meus, -a, -um_ (my), _tuus_ (your) and _noster_ (our) are adjectives, so they agree with the noun in gender, number and case: _pater meus_ (my father), _māter mea_ (my mother), _frātrēs meī_ (my brothers). Some nouns follow a third pattern, the third declension: _pater, māter, mīles, rēx_ and _homō_ have different endings (_patrēs, mātrēs, mīlitēs_) which you will learn simply by meeting them. Adjectives such as _fortis_ (brave) and _tristis_ (sad) use the same endings for masculine and feminine.

units.title: Where, and with whom
units.intro: To say where someone does something, use _in_ plus the ablative: _puer in hortō ambulat_ (the boy walks in the garden). To say who is with you, or who is missing, use _cum_ (with) or _sine_ (without), which also take the ablative: _cum amīcō_, _sine amīcō_. Remember that Latin endings, not word order, do the work: the ablative ending is what tells you 'in the garden' rather than 'the garden' as an object.

units.title: To, from, through
units.blurb: ad, in, ex, per, trans, prope + the right case
units.intro: Prepositions decide the case. _in_ with the ablative means 'in', but _in_ with the accusative means 'into': _in hortō_ (in the garden) vs _in hortum_ (into the garden). _ad_ (to) and _per_ (through), _trans_ (across) and _prope_ (near) take the accusative; _ex_ (out of) takes the ablative. When you meet a new preposition, learn it together with its case.

units.title: How many?
units.blurb: Numbers one to ten with plural nouns
units.intro: Numbers from four to ten never change: _quattuor, quīnque, sex, septem, octō, novem, decem_. Two and three do change: _duo, duae, duo_ (two) and _trēs, trēs, tria_ (three) match the gender of what is counted. After a number, the noun stays in the case the sentence needs: _trēs puerī in hortō sunt_ (three boys are in the garden). _quot?_ asks 'how many?'.

units.title: Counting and time
units.blurb: One, eleven to twenty, and telling the hour
units.intro: _ūnus, ūna, ūnum_ (one) is declined like an adjective: _ūnus puer_, _ūna puella_. The numbers eleven to twenty never change, like four to ten: _ūndecim, duodecim, trēdecim_ and on up to _vīgintī_ (twenty). To ask the time, say _Quota hōra est?_ (literally “what number hour is it?”) and answer with an ordinal number, which agrees with _hōra_: _Hōra tertia est_ (it is the third hour). To say AT an hour, put _hōra_ and the ordinal in the ablative: _hōrā tertiā_.

units.title: Whose is it?
units.blurb: The genitive: of the boy, of the boys
units.intro: The genitive case says who owns something or who is related to someone. It is the “'s” of English: _liber puerī_ (the boy's book), _liber puerōrum_ (the boys' book), _fīlia Mārcī_ (Marcus's daughter). First-declension genitive: _-ae_ (singular), _-ārum_ (plural). Second declension: _-ī_ and _-ōrum_. Third declension: _-is_ and _-um_. _Cuius?_ asks “whose?”.

units.title: Giving and telling
units.intro: The dative case marks the person who receives something, the indirect object, “to” or “for”: _pater fīliō librum dat_ (the father gives a book to the son). Endings: first declension _-ae_ / _-īs_, second _-ō_ / _-īs_, third _-ī_ / _-ibus_. The pronouns have their own forms: _mihi_ (to me), _tibi_ (to you), _nōbīs_ (to us), _vōbīs_ (to you all). _Cui?_ asks “to whom?”.
